tools.description: Persist a conclusion you have personally reviewed about a specific file and line range. Supply `path` (any path in the active project, to select the database), `file` (project-relative path of the file), `line_start`/`line_end` (one-based inclusive), plus `severity`, `category`, `title`, and `description` (all your own judgment — SlugAudit never generates these). The finding is bound to the file's current content hash and auto-invalidates (status becomes stale) the moment that file changes, so findings never outlive the source they were about. Use this to record reviewed issues, not raw diagnostics.

category.description: Category label for the finding, e.g. security/performance/correctness/style

description.description: Detailed description of the finding, its impact, and any remediation (max 10000 chars)

file.description: Project-relative path of the file this finding is about

line_end.description: One-based inclusive end line of the finding

line_start.description: One-based inclusive start line of the finding

path.description: Any path inside the active project, used to select the database

severity.description: Severity of the finding, e.g. critical/high/medium/low/informational

title.description: Concise one-line title summarizing the finding (max 200 chars)

tools.title: Record a finding

Safer than querying the findings table directly through `query`, which returns every session's rows. Supply `path` (any path in the active project) to select the database, and optionally `file` to filter to a specific file.

file.description:
Optional project-relative file path. When supplied, only findings
for that file are returned. Omit to return all current-session
findings for the project.

path.description: Any path inside the active project

tools.name: finding_read

FindingReadEntry.description:
One finding row, scoped to the current agent session. Every field is
exactly what the `finding` tool stored — SlugAudit never generates
any of this text.

tools.title: Read session findings

tools.description: Operational snapshot: watcher health, unreconciled event counts, last verified sequence, current revision id and file count, parser pack version, and process-wide tool-call counters. Intended for operators/health checks; safe to call repeatedly and never mutates state. Call `project_control` with `"on"` on a path first to surface per-project database state; calling without a path returns global counters and the most-recently-touched project's watcher health only.

path.description:
Optional project root. When omitted, returns watcher state for
every project currently registered with the server and skips the
per-database stats. When supplied, returns stats for that project:
watcher state if the project is registered with the server's
watcher, database state if the project's database exists, and the
counters otherwise. Reading is strictly read-only — this tool
never syncs, never registers a watch, and never writes, so a
health check can never perturb the state it is reporting on.

tools.name: health

DatabaseState.description:
What the project database holds.

Read as one unit: one failed query leaves the whole object absent rather
than producing a revision alongside a count that didn't come back, so a
caller never has to detect a half-read answer — there isn't one to
detect. That is also why no field here is a sentinel: absence is the
`None` on [`HealthResponse::database`], not a magic number inside it.

file_count.description:
Files in the database — every discovered file, including rows with
`file_kind = 'skipped'`; `skipped_file_count` breaks those out.

parser_pack_version.description:
Parser pack version stored on the current revision. `None` if no
revision has been published yet.

revision_id.description:
`revision_id` of the current revision. `None` if nothing has been
published yet.

skipped_file_count.description:
Of `file_count`, how many rows were discovered but never read
(`file_kind = 'skipped'`: oversize or unreadable), so they hold no
content. `file_count - skipped_file_count` is the number of files
that were actually read.

HealthPhase.description:
Coarse-grained operational phase. Derived from existing state rather
than tracked separately so it can't drift.

- `Importing`: no current revision — the first sync has never succeeded.
- `Restoring`: watcher is `NeedsVerification` or `Desynced`; the next
  call will do a full verification rather than incremental reconcile.
- `SteadyState`: watcher `Healthy`, no unreconciled events, a current
  revision exists, the project is fully served from disk.
- `Unavailable`: watcher could not be initialized; every call will
  full-publish.
- `NoActiveProject`: server has been initialized but no `ensure_current`
  call has succeeded, so the watcher state can't be summarized.
- `IndexedUnwatched`: the enabled project has a published revision in
  its database, but this server has no registered watcher for that path.
  Indexed evidence remains readable; no watcher health is implied.
- `Disabled`: `request.path` resolved to no enabled project — the
  activation marker is absent — so nothing can serve that path until
  `project_control` enables it. `remedy` names that call. This is a
  state, not an error: a diagnostic tool that fails when there is
  nothing to diagnose is useless.

ServerCounters.description:
Counters for this server process since it started.

Operational instrumentation: these exist so the tool's own behaviour can
be measured over time. Nothing here is something a caller acts on, which
is why they share one object and drive no `phase` or `remedy`.

consecutive_full_publishes.description:
How many consecutive full publishes (untrusted-watcher or
Unavailable-path verifications) have run since the last successful
incremental reconcile. A value that persists at 1+ across calls
means the watcher is not being trusted — e.g. Linux inotify
`fs.inotify.max_user_watches` overflow forcing `Desynced` — so
every tool call full-publishes. See the full-publish runbook
in `docs/TROUBLESHOOTING.md`.

last_sync_duration_ms.description:
Duration of the most recent successful `ensure_current`, in
milliseconds. Zero before the first sync.

last_sync_unix_seconds.description:
Unix-epoch seconds of the most recent successful `ensure_current`
across the entire server's lifetime. Zero before the first sync.

tool_call_count.description: Total tool calls served since process start.

tool_call_error_count.description: Total tool calls that returned any `ErrorData` since process start.

tool_call_total_ms.description: Sum of every tool call's work duration, in milliseconds.

SystemMemoryInfo.description:
Host memory as measured at startup (or the conservative fallback,
reported by `detect_system_memory` when it could not be measured).
Surfaced in the `health` response because it sizes the Adaptive
profile's import budget.

available_bytes.description: Memory available to this process for import budgets, in bytes.

WatcherHealth.description:
Health of a project's filesystem watcher. Never silently assume healthy —
the caller must check before trusting the dirty set.

Derived `Serialize` so the `health` MCP tool can return this enum as
part of its `Json<HealthResponse>` response. Derived `JsonSchema` so
the same schema is surfaced through MCP to consumers.

oneOf.description: Watcher is active and events are being recorded.

Watcher history is untrustworthy (e.g. after restart). The current
filesystem must be reconciled against the stored state before the
database can be considered synchronized.

Watcher detected an integrity problem (queue overflow, watch removed,
etc.). A full verification is required before serving evidence.

Watcher could not be initialized for this project (e.g. platform
doesn't support it, or the project root isn't watchable).

WatcherState.description: The watcher's view of the supervised project.

last_verified_sequence.description: The sequence acknowledged by the most recent reconcile.

pending_dirty.description:
Unreconciled dirty paths — modified or created since the last
successful reconcile.

database.description:
What the project database holds. `None` if the project has never
been synced, or if the database could not be read. Either every
field inside is present or the whole object is absent: a partial
read is not representable, so no number here is ever a placeholder.

phase.description:
Coarse classification of what the server is doing right now.
Derivation rule documented on [`HealthPhase`].

remedy.description:
The next action to take when no project is being served by this
answer: the same static sentence the `project_not_enabled` error
carries in `ErrorData.data.remedy`, so a caller can treat "health
says `disabled`" and "every tool fails with `project_not_enabled`"
as one instruction. `Some` exactly when `phase` is `disabled`, or
when no `path` was supplied and this server has no project at all;
`None` whenever a project is actually being served.

server.description: What this server process has done since it started.

system_memory.description:
Host physical and available memory. Reported because it sets the
adaptive profile's import budget (`src/model/profile.rs`), so a
caller that trips `max_total_import_bytes` can see what sized it.

watcher.description:
What the filesystem watcher knows about the supervised project.
`None` only if no project is currently registered with the server.
The fields are one object because they become unknowable together —
there is no state in which half of them exist.

tools.title: Operational health

tools.description: Want somewhere to start? Mechanical facts extracted from the index — call sites by callee name (unwrap, expect, panic, todo, unimplemented, assert), diagnostics, TODO/FIXME/HACK comment markers, and credential-shaped files. Nothing here is judged, ranked, scored, or ordered by importance: every item is a fact, and deciding which of them matter is entirely your call. Call with only `path` to get every mechanic with its row count, its distinct-file count (`files`) and `covers` (`rust_only` means a zero count is unchecked, not absent), then call again with one `mechanic` id to get file/line rows, optionally narrowed with `pattern` (a path GLOB, e.g. `src/auth/*`; without `*`/`?` it is a substring match). A rows response always reports `returned`/`total` and `complete` plus the file denominators `files_total`/`files_covered`; there is no row cap, so a page is cut only by your `limit` (omit it for everything that fits) and by the page byte size (64 KiB by default; `page_bytes` raises it up to the server ceiling, reported as `row_budget_bytes`/`rows_bytes`, with `limited_by` naming what stopped it). To page, pass `offset` = `next_offset` together with `expected_revision` = the previous page's `revision_id`: a changed index is then refused with `stale_revision` instead of silently skipping or repeating rows. For `mechanic`/`file`/`line` triples with no per-row text, pass `mode: compact`; with only `path` it then enumerates every mechanic in one response under the same completeness fields — the cheap way to see the whole surface.

LeadMode.description: How a response renders its rows. See [`LeadsResponse::rows`].

oneOf.description: Each row carries its `detail` text (clipped; see [`LeadRow`]).
Each row is a [`CompactLeadRow`]: no per-row text at all.

expected_revision.description: Pin the revision a resumed page expects; a mismatch is refused

limit.description: Max rows in this page; omit for everything that fits the byte budget

mechanic.description: Optional mechanic id; omit for counts only

page_bytes.description: Page size in bytes of serialized rows; omit for the server default, clamped to the ceiling (reported)

path.description: Any path inside the active project, used to select the database

pattern.description: Optional path GLOB filter (substring match when it has no `*`/`?`)

tools.name: leads

CompactLeadRow.description:
One row of a compact page: which mechanic observed what, at a path and
line. No text is carried — read the file, or ask for `mode: full` — which
is what makes a whole-surface sweep affordable.

file.description: Project-relative path of the file the observation is in.

line.description: One-based start line, or `0` when the evidence carries no span.

mechanic.description:
The mechanic this row belongs to — an id from `mechanic_counts`, and
the id to pass as `mechanic` for that mechanic's `detail` text.

FileCount.description: One file's share of a page, in first-appearance order.

count.description:
Rows of this mechanic in *this page* that belong to this file — not
the file's total, which is what `files_total` / `files_covered`
track across pages.

LeadRow.description:
One lead observation: file, line (0 when the evidence carries no span),
and the mechanic's own clipped detail text.

detail.description:
The mechanic's own text: callee text, diagnostic message, or comment
text. Empty for path-shaped mechanics. Clipped to `MAX_DETAIL_CHARS`
characters when longer — check `detail_clipped`.

detail_clipped.description:
True when `detail` was clipped to `MAX_DETAIL_CHARS`; the text is then
a prefix of the stored evidence and the remainder exists only in the
file itself. False means the whole stored text is present.

file.description: Project-relative path of the file the observation is in.

line.description: One-based start line, or `0` when the evidence carries no span.

LeadRows.description:
The rows of a page, shaped by the request's `mode`; one response carries
one variant, never a mix. `full` (the default) is [`LeadRow`] with its
`detail` text; `compact` is [`CompactLeadRow`] with no per-row text. All
the envelope's completeness fields mean the same thing either way.

MechanicCount.description:
One mechanic's complete counts under the request's pattern — complete
regardless of paging, with no ordering by importance.

count.description:
How many observations this mechanic has in the current revision
under the same `pattern`. Complete, never paged.

covers.description:
The languages this count covers. `rust_only` with a zero count on a
non-Rust project means nothing was checked.

files.description:
Distinct files containing at least one observation. This is the
denominator to enumerate: a 50,000-row mechanic is usually far fewer
files, and a file is the unit a sweep can finish.

mechanic.description: Stable id — pass it back as `mechanic` to get this mechanic's rows.

MechanicCoverage.description:
Which languages a mechanic was actually measured over. A zero count on a
[`MechanicCoverage::RustOnly`] mechanic means *unchecked*, not *absent* —
without this field that distinction is only prose.

oneOf.description: Only the Rust call walker produces the evidence this mechanic reads.

PageLimit.description:
What stopped a page. Reports the cap that acted; never a judgment about
whether the page was the right size.

oneOf.description: The mechanic was exhausted: `complete` is true.
The caller's `limit` was reached; more rows exist.

The response byte budget was reached; more rows exist. Raise
`limit` if one was set, or page on.

complete.description:
True when this page reaches the end of the scope
(`offset + returned >= total`), and when a `full` call requested no
mechanic. False means rows remain and `next_offset` is present.

files_covered.description:
Distinct files represented in rows `0..offset + returned` of the
scope. Cumulative for a sweep at one revision, because rows are
ordered by path and a page boundary can split a file but never
reorder the files. `files_total - files_covered` is what is left.

files_total.description:
Distinct files holding at least one observation of any mechanic in
scope — the denominator a sweep can exhaust. `0` when a `full` call
requested no mechanic. For a single mechanic it equals that
`mechanic_counts` entry's `files`.

limited_by.description:
What stopped the page: the scope ended, the caller's `limit`, or the
byte budget.

mechanic_counts.description:
Every mechanic this revision can answer under the request's
`pattern`, with its row and distinct-file counts and what it covers.
Counts are complete regardless of `limit`/`offset`, and carry no
ordering by importance — the order is the fixed declaration order.

next_offset.description:
Pass as `offset` on the next call while `complete` is false, with
`expected_revision` set to this response's `revision_id`.

oversized_row.description:
True when `rows_bytes` exceeds `row_budget_bytes` because the first
row alone is larger than the page. It is returned whole so paging
makes progress and nothing is lost.

page_bytes_clamped_from.description:
Non-null when the requested (or configured default) page size exceeded
`max_query_response_bytes` and was clamped: the size that was asked
for. `row_budget_bytes` is then the ceiling.

page_file_counts.description: Rows grouped per file for this page only.

revision_id.description:
Revision the counts and rows were read from. Pass it as
`expected_revision` on the next page to have a changed index refused
rather than mis-paged.

row_budget_bytes.description:
Serialized-JSON byte budget applied to `rows` this call: the
request's `page_bytes` or the server default
(`SLUGAUDIT_DEFAULT_PAGE_BYTES`), clamped to the ceiling
`max_query_response_bytes`, the same page size `query` spends. One row
is always returned even if it alone exceeds it (see `oversized_row`).

rows.description:
The page's rows, shaped by the request's `mode`. Empty when a `full`
call supplied no `mechanic`; a `compact` call with no `mechanic`
enumerates every mechanic instead, one triple per row.

rows_bytes.description:
Serialized-JSON bytes of the returned `rows`, measured per row
exactly as `query` measures its values. The rest of this envelope
(`mechanic_counts` — at most one entry per mechanic — and
`page_file_counts`) is additional and small relative to the rows.

total.description:
Total rows in the enumerated scope — the requested mechanic, or (in
`compact` mode with no `mechanic`) every mechanic — under the same
`pattern`; `0` when a `full` call requested no mechanic.

tools.title: Mechanical leads

tools.description: Enable or disable SlugAudit for a project. Pass `action` = `"on"` to enable a project (creates the activation directory and runs the initial import), or `"off"` to disable it (removes the activation directory and purges its database). On `"on"` the runtime directory `.planning/slugaudit/` is also appended to the project-root `.gitignore` unless a rule that already ignores it is present; the response's `gitignore` field reports `added`, `already_ignored`, or `not_written` plus the file's path. `"off"` never edits `.gitignore`. Supply `path` to target a specific project root; defaults to the current directory. If the project was moved, copied, or re-extracted elsewhere (e.g. unzipped fresh from an archive), a stale `.planning/slugaudit/project.db` is discarded and rebuilt from source automatically — the agent does not need to delete it or re-enable manually.

ProjectControlAction.description: The action to take — on enables, off disables.

action.description: Action to perform: `"on"` enables the project, `"off"` disables it.

path.description: Project root path. Defaults to the current directory when omitted.

profile.description: Optional audit profile to configure: `"audit"`, `"lean"`, or `"adaptive"`.

tools.name: project_control

GitignoreReport.description: What enabling a project did about its root `.gitignore`.

error.description: Why nothing was written. Present only for `"not_written"`.

path.description: Absolute path of the project-root `.gitignore` that was inspected.

status.description:
One of `"added"` (the ignore rule was appended), `"already_ignored"`
(an equivalent rule was present; file untouched), or `"not_written"`
(the file was left untouched and the project is enabled anyway).

GitignoreStatus.description: Outcome of the `.gitignore` guard, as a closed set.

ImportReport.description: Summary of an initial import that ran on enable.

gitignore.description:
What `"on"` did about the project-root `.gitignore`. Absent for
`"off"`, which never touches that file.

import.description: Present when action was `"on"` and an initial import ran.

path.description: Absolute path of the project root that was affected.

tools.title: Enable or disable a project

tools.description: Query the indexed codebase with read-only SQL. Key tables: files (id, path, language, byte_len, content — full text of every indexed file including non-code files), evidence (id, file_id, kind, start_line, end_line, payload — Symbol, Import, Comment, Structure), dependency_edges (from_file_id, to_file_id, raw_import_text, resolution_kind, confidence, syntax_unmodeled). To inspect code or file content directly from the DB without filesystem reads, query `files.content` (e.g. `SELECT content FROM files WHERE path = 'src/main.rs'`); `line_count(text)` and `line_range(text, start, end)` read a file by 1-based lines, and an oversized first row is clipped with a `substr` continuation in `clipped_cells`. To link evidence to file paths, always JOIN: `SELECT f.path, e.start_line FROM evidence e JOIN files f ON e.file_id = f.id WHERE e.kind = 'Symbol' AND json_extract(e.payload, '$.name') = 'configure'`. Schema discovery: `SELECT name FROM sqlite_master WHERE type='table'`.

expected_revision.description:
Set to the previous page's `revision_id` when resuming a sweep. If
the index changed since that page, the call is refused with the
`stale_revision` code instead of returning a page whose ordering no
longer matches the offset: `files`/`evidence` hold only the current
revision, so a stored offset means nothing once the tree changes.

offset.description:
Number of matching rows to skip when paging through a result.
Combined with the response's `next_offset`, and valid only while
the revision id stays the same across pages (see [`QueryResponse`]).

page_bytes.description:
Page size in serialized JSON bytes. Omit it for the server default
(64 KiB unless configured otherwise; the response's `page_bytes` says
what applied). A larger value returns a larger page, up to the hard
ceiling `max_query_response_bytes`: a value above the ceiling is
clamped and the response reports `page_bytes_clamped_from`. Pages are
cut on a row boundary; when the first row alone is larger than the page,
its TEXT/BLOB cells are clipped to fit and listed in `clipped_cells`
with the `substr` expression that continues each one. Raise
`page_bytes` to avoid clipping.

path.description: Any path inside the active project.

sql.description:
Read-only SQL against the project's own database — arbitrary joins,
CTEs, and window functions are fine. Only writes are rejected, and
that comes from the connection itself, not from inspecting this
text: there is no keyword blocklist or table allowlist.

tools.name: query

ClippedCell.description: One TEXT or BLOB cell that was cut to fit the page.

column.description: Result column name of the clipped cell.

continue_with.description:
A ready-to-use expression for the rest, `substr("<column>", start,
length)`. The column name is quoted as an identifier; apply the same
`substr` to the expression that produced the column.

next_start.description: 1-based position of the first unit not returned, ready for `substr`.

returned.description: How many units of the value the response carries (from the start).

row.description:
Zero-based index of the row in the whole result (`offset` plus its
position on the page), the same numbering `offset` uses.

total.description: How many units the whole value has: SQLite's `length(value)`.

unit.description:
What `returned`, `total` and `next_start` count, in `substr`'s own
units: `"characters"` for text, `"bytes"` for a blob, and `"bytes"` for
a text containing a NUL (SQLite's text functions stop at a NUL, so such
a value is continued as bytes: `continue_with` casts it to a blob and
the rest comes back hex-encoded).

column.description: Result column name of the cell.

row.description:
Zero-based index of the row in the whole result (`offset` plus its
position on the page), the same numbering `offset` uses.

clipped_cells.description:
The TEXT/BLOB cells cut from the first row because the row alone was
larger than `page_bytes`; empty when nothing was cut. Each entry gives
the absolute `row` index, `column`, `returned` and `total` length in
`substr` units (characters for text, bytes for a blob), `next_start`
(1-based) and a ready `continue_with` expression. No data is lost: the
rest of every clipped cell is one `substr` away. If this is empty,
every cell is complete. Only a row whose non-text cells alone exceed
the page (or a page smaller than one character per cell) can leave
`rows_bytes` above `page_bytes`.

next_offset.description:
Use this as the next request's `offset` when present. Only valid
while `revision_id` is unchanged (see the paging contract above).

non_finite_cells.description:
REAL cells that are `null` in `rows` only because JSON cannot carry an
infinity: each entry gives the absolute `row`, the `column` and the real
`value` (`"Infinity"`, `"-Infinity"` or `"NaN"`). A `null` that is not
listed here is SQL NULL. Empty when every REAL is finite.

page_bytes.description:
The page size that applied to this call, in serialized JSON bytes: the
request's `page_bytes` or the server default, clamped to the ceiling.

page_bytes_clamped_from.description:
Non-null when the requested (or configured default) page size exceeded
`max_query_response_bytes` and was clamped: the size that was asked
for. `page_bytes` is then the ceiling.

revision_id.description:
Revision id the page was read from. Compare across pages to detect
a revision change that invalidates `next_offset` paging, or pass it
back as `expected_revision` to have the change refused.

rows_bytes.description: Serialized JSON bytes of the returned `rows`, measured per row.

total_rows.description:
Exact row count of the whole result, ignoring `offset` and the page
cut, computed by SQLite over the same statement. Null only when
counting exhausted its budget; `total_rows_unavailable` then says why.
Never an estimate.

total_rows_unavailable.description:
Why `total_rows` is null (the budget that stopped the count); null
whenever `total_rows` is present.

tools.title: Read-only SQL query

tools.description: Automatic project snapshot: file/language counts, parser failures, evidence-kind counts, open findings, and inbound/outbound dependency-edge counts. Use this first to understand the project's shape, then query for specifics. No score, no risk leads.

path.description: Any path inside the active project: its root, or a file/directory under it.

tools.name: report

CompletenessCount.description: Row count for one extraction-completeness value.

extraction_completeness.description:
One of `Full`, `Partial`, `ContentOnly`, `Unavailable`. `ContentOnly`
means the file's text is in `files.content` but no parser ran over it
— the file is readable even though it has no structural evidence.
`Unavailable` means no content is retained at all (binary, or skipped).

CompletenessEnvelope.description: Counts that say whether the rest of the response is the whole truth.

evidence_capped_file_count.description:
Files whose stored evidence was cut short by an evidence cap: each
carries the `evidence:truncated` diagnostic appended by
`sync::sample::apply_evidence_limits`. Their structural record is
incomplete in a way this report cannot recover, so an agent counting
`evidence_counts` for them is counting a floor, not a total.

extraction_completeness_counts.description:
Every `files` row by `extraction_completeness`, so "text present but
not parsed" (`ContentOnly`) is visible as itself instead of vanishing
into a parser-failure count.

file_class_counts.description:
Every `files` row by `file_class` — where the code came from, derived
from the path alone (`sync::classify`): `authored` (the project's own
source), `generated` (a machine-written file: a `generated` path token
or a codegen suffix such as `.pb.go` / `.g.dart` / `.min.js`), or
`vendored` (a third-party tree: `vendor/`, `node_modules/`, …). A
mechanic whose rows are dominated by one class can be summarised in a
sentence instead of paged row by row. `vendored` subsumes `generated`
when a path matches both. A path heuristic, not a verdict: it says
where a file came from, never whether it matters.

index_partial.description:
True when the index does not cover every file the last publish
discovered — i.e. `skipped_file_count > 0`. False means every
discovered file is represented by a row here.

indexed_files_without_evidence.description:
`indexed` rows with no evidence at all — content is present and
readable, but the index holds nothing structural about them (a
language with no loaded parser, or a file that parsed to nothing).
Binary and skipped rows are excluded: no evidence is their expected
state, not a gap.

skipped_by_reason.description:
Those skipped rows grouped by `skip_reason`. This is the "why" paired
with `index_partial`; a file the walk could not even name (a non-UTF-8
path) has no representable `files.path` and cannot appear here — it is
visible only in the publish report and the server log.

skipped_file_count.description:
`files` rows with `file_kind = 'skipped'`, i.e. files that exist in the
project but are not in the index.

DependencyEdgeTotals.description: Edge totals in both directions, over the whole revision.

inbound_edge_count.description:
Edges whose `to_file_id` names a row in `files` — the subset that
lands on a project file. `Unresolved` and `External` edges carry no
target, and `import_resolution` splits those two apart; this total
groups them only by their absence of a target.

inbound_file_count.description: Distinct files that are the target of at least one edge.

outbound_edge_count.description:
`count(*) FROM dependency_edges`: every edge, since every edge
originates at a file (`from_file_id` is `NOT NULL`).

outbound_file_count.description: Distinct files that are the source of at least one edge.

EvidenceKindCount.description: How many evidence rows the current revision holds for one kind.

ImportResolutionCount.description:
How many import edges fell into each resolution bucket. A project with
mostly `External` and `Unresolved` edges and very few `Resolved` ones
has an import graph the evidence can't connect — useful context for an
AI deciding how much to trust dependency traversal for this project.

LanguageCount.description:
How many discovered files the last revision attributed to one detected
language.

ParserFailureFile.description:
A file whose parse failed or was not attempted, with enough detail for
an AI to decide whether the failure is worth investigating or just
noise (e.g. a `.claude_output.txt` scratch file that should have been
excluded, vs. a real source file with a genuine syntax error).

extraction_completeness.description:
One of `Full`, `Partial`, `ContentOnly`, `Unavailable`. `ContentOnly`
means the file's text *is* indexed but no parser ran over it — the
row is listed for availability reasons, not because extraction
failed, and its content can still be read from `files.content`.

parse_error_reason.description:
Set only when the parser returned a hard error (not just syntax
error nodes). `None` for `NotAttempted` and `SyntaxErrors`.

parser_availability.description:
One of `Available`, `Unavailable`, `LoadFailed`. Separates
`ContentOnly` rows that have no parser for their language
(`Unavailable`) from ones whose parser could not be loaded
(`LoadFailed`), which a completeness value alone cannot.

SkipReasonCount.description: Row count for one recorded skip reason.

reason.description:
A short stable code from `files.skip_reason`: `oversize` (over the
per-file import ceiling), `unreadable` (the read failed) or
`stat_failed` (the stat failed, so `files.byte_len` is NULL: size
unknown, not 0). Empty when a skipped row carries no recorded reason.

completeness.description:
Whether every count above is the whole truth: rows by kind, skipped
rows by reason, rows by extraction completeness, and a partial-index
flag. See [`CompletenessEnvelope`].

credential_pattern_file_count.description:
How many rows in `files` match common credential-file patterns
(`.env`, `*.pem`, `*.key`, `id_rsa*`, etc. — the same list the
SQL below matches, and the same list `leads`' `credential_files`
rows use). SlugAudit records these paths like any other file —
including when the file was skipped and no content was retained —
so this count makes the AI aware it is handling credential-*looking*
paths even when it cannot read them.

dependency_edges.description:
The same graph counted in both directions: how many edges leave a
file, how many land on one, and how many files are on each end.
Pure arithmetic over `dependency_edges` — no ranking, no severity,
and no claim about which file matters. Per-file traversal is the
`slugaudit://queries/blast_radius.sql` recipe.

diagnostic_count.description:
Total number of Diagnostic evidence items (e.g. linter or compiler
diagnostics extracted from source files).

file_count.description:
Rows in `files`: every file the last publish discovered, whether or
not it was indexed. Read `completeness.file_kind_counts` to see how
many of those have content (`indexed`), are binary, or were skipped —
this number alone does not mean "files with evidence".

import_resolution.description:
How many import edges are Resolved vs Unresolved vs External — a
key asymmetry signal. A project with mostly External/Unresolved
imports has a disconnected import graph that dependency traversal
can't help with.

parser_failure_files.description:
Up to `MAX_PARSER_FAILURE_FILES` files with parse failures, so the
AI can see whether failures are concentrated in scratch/temp files
(noise) or in real source files (worth investigating).

parser_failure_files_total.description:
Uncapped total of files matching the `parser_failure_files` predicate.
Larger than the returned list's length means the list was truncated at
`MAX_PARSER_FAILURE_FILES`; equal means the list is complete.

unsupported_language_unresolved_count.description:
Of the `Unresolved` count in `import_resolution`, how many come from
import syntax the resolver couldn't parse at all — `extract_reference`
returned `None` on the raw text (e.g. Go's `import "fmt"`), as
opposed to an import whose syntax was parsed but matched no project
file (e.g. a stdlib module like `kotlin.math.max`). SlugAudit
records both as `Unresolved` edges since it can't tell them apart
at resolution time, but they mean very different things: a high
count here means "this project's import syntax isn't modeled yet,"
not "this project's imports are broken."

tools.title: Project snapshot

tools.description: Inspect and extract code AST structures from a file or across the project using Tree-sitter. Specify `file` to search a single file, or omit `file` and specify `language` (with optional `pattern`) to search across matching project files. Returns matched AST nodes with `file`, `start_line`, `end_line`, and `text` snippet. The `query` must name at least one capture with `@name`. Examples: Rust `(function_item name: (identifier) @name body: (block) @body)`, Python `(function_definition name: (identifier) @name body: (block) @body)`, TypeScript/JS `(function_declaration name: (identifier) @name)`, or whole-node `(class_definition) @cls`.

expected_revision.description:
Set to a previous page's `revision_id` when resuming; if the index
changed since, the call is refused instead of paging a shifted order.

file.description:
Project-relative path of a single file to match against.
When omitted, matches all files in the project matching `language`.

full_text.description:
Whether to include full matched source text up to MAX_TEXT_BYTES.
Defaults to true for single-file queries, and false (lean 1-line snippet) for multi-file queries.

language.description:
Language grammar to use (e.g. "rust", "python", "typescript").
Required when `file` is omitted; optional if `file` is provided.

offset.description:
Number of matches to skip when paging through a result; use the
previous response's `next_offset`. Valid only while `revision_id` is
unchanged, and only together with the same `start_after_file`.

page_bytes.description:
Page size in serialized JSON bytes of `matches`. Omit it for the server
default (64 KiB unless configured otherwise; the response's
`page_bytes` says what applied). A value above the hard ceiling
`max_query_response_bytes` is clamped and reported as
`page_bytes_clamped_from`. Pages are cut on a match boundary; the first
match is always returned, so a single match larger than the page
arrives whole (its own `text_truncated` flag covers the 1 MB text cap).

path.description: Any path inside the active project.

pattern.description: Optional path pattern (e.g. "*auth*", "src/**/*.rs") to filter files.

query.description:
A tree-sitter S-expression query, e.g. `(function_item name: (identifier) @name)`.
For patterns normalized evidence and `query` can't easily express.

start_after_file.description:
Multi-file queries only: scan only files whose path sorts strictly
after this one. Use the previous response's `next_start_after_file`
when it reports `files_not_scanned`.

tools.name: structure

StructureMatch.description:
One capture match mapped back to source coordinates, with the
clipping/extraction flags that bound its `text`.

bytes_not_scanned.description: Content bytes of those unscanned files.

files_not_scanned.description:
Multi-file only: matching files past the memory window that were NOT
scanned by this call (0 means every matching file after
`start_after_file` was scanned). When above 0 the result is incomplete
even if `truncated` is false: finish `next_offset` paging, then repeat
with `start_after_file` = `next_start_after_file` and offset 0.

matches_bytes.description: Serialized JSON bytes of the returned `matches`.

next_offset.description:
Pass as the next request's `offset` (with the same other fields) when
present.

page_bytes.description: The page size that applied, in serialized JSON bytes of `matches`.

page_bytes_clamped_from.description:
Non-null when the requested (or configured default) page size exceeded
`max_query_response_bytes`: the size asked for; `page_bytes` is then
the ceiling.

truncated.description:
True when more matches exist past this page (page bytes or the match
cap); `next_offset` continues. False means this scan window is done.

unparsed_files.description:
Multi-file only: files the parser produced no syntax tree for, so they
contributed no matches. Empty when none.
